learningObjectives.title: Cooking of food and heat transfer
Functional and chemical properties of food
Food spoilage, contamination and food safety

questions.q: What are the three methods by which heat is transferred to food during cooking?
questions.explain: Heat is transferred to food by conduction, convection and radiation.

questions.q: Which method of heat transfer occurs when warmer, less dense particles in a liquid or gas rise and cooler particles sink, setting up a current?
questions.explain: Convection moves heat through circulating currents in liquids and gases such as water or air in an oven.

questions.q: Frying an egg, where heat passes directly from the hot pan into the egg by contact, is an example of which type of heat transfer?
questions.explain: Conduction transfers heat by direct contact between the hot pan and the food touching it.

questions.q: Grilling and toasting cook food mainly by which method of heat transfer?
questions.explain: Grilling and toasting use infrared radiation, transferring heat in waves without direct contact.

questions.q: What is the name of the process in which starch granules swell, burst and thicken a liquid when heated in the presence of water?
questions.explain: Gelatinisation is the thickening of a liquid as starch granules absorb water, swell and burst on heating.

questions.q: At approximately what temperature do egg proteins begin to coagulate (set) when cooked?
questions.explain: Egg proteins denature and coagulate at around 60–70°C, causing the egg to set.

questions.q: What is the name of the process where starch is broken down to dextrins by dry heat, giving toast and bread crusts their brown colour?
questions.explain: Dextrinisation is the browning of starchy foods under dry heat as starch converts to dextrins.

questions.q: The Maillard reaction, which browns seared meat and bread crusts, is a reaction between which two components?
questions.explain: The Maillard reaction is a non-enzymic browning between amino acids and reducing sugars when heated.

questions.q: What is the name of the process where sugar breaks down and turns golden-brown when heated to a high temperature?
questions.explain: Caramelisation is the browning of sugar as it breaks down at high temperatures.

questions.q: Which natural emulsifier found in egg yolk allows oil and water to combine, for example in mayonnaise?
questions.explain: Lecithin in egg yolk acts as an emulsifier, holding oil and water together in a stable mixture.

questions.q: Why does adding fat to a pastry mixture (shortening) produce a crumbly texture?
options: The fat coats the flour and limits gluten formation
The fat makes the gluten strands longer and stronger
The fat causes the starch to gelatinise
The fat traps air bubbles to aerate the mixture
questions.explain: In shortening, fat coats the flour particles so less gluten develops, giving a short, crumbly texture.

questions.q: A student slices apples for a fruit salad and notices the cut surfaces turning brown. Which action would best prevent this enzymic browning?
options: Coat the slices in lemon juice
Leave the slices at room temperature
Add a little salt to the slices
questions.explain: The acid in lemon juice slows the enzyme responsible for browning on the cut fruit surfaces.

questions.q: A student wants to thicken a white sauce. Which ingredient and process should they rely on?
questions.explain: Starch from the flour gelatinises in the hot liquid, absorbing water and thickening the sauce.

questions.q: What is the temperature range of the 'danger zone' in which bacteria multiply most rapidly?
questions.explain: The danger zone is 5°C to 63°C, the range in which bacteria multiply most quickly.

questions.q: Why should cooked food be heated to a core temperature of at least 75°C?
options: To ensure harmful bacteria are destroyed
To speed up gelatinisation of starch
questions.explain: Reaching a core temperature of 75°C kills most harmful bacteria, making food safe to eat.

questions.q: Which bacteria are most commonly associated with raw poultry and eggs?
questions.explain: Salmonella is commonly linked to raw poultry and eggs and is a frequent cause of food poisoning.

questions.q: What does a 'use by' date on a food product indicate?
options: The date after which the food may be unsafe to eat
The date after which the food is simply less fresh but still safe
The date the food was manufactured
The best date to freeze the food
questions.explain: A 'use by' date relates to safety, whereas a 'best before' date relates to quality.

questions.q: Which set of conditions do bacteria need in order to multiply?
questions.explain: Bacteria multiply when they have warmth, moisture, food and enough time.

questions.q: To reduce the risk of cross-contamination when storing food in a fridge, where should raw meat be placed?
options: On the bottom shelf below other foods
On the top shelf above cooked foods
In the door with the drinks
questions.explain: Storing raw meat on the bottom shelf stops its juices dripping onto and contaminating other foods.

questions.q: Cooked rice is left out at room temperature overnight and eaten the next day, causing illness. Which bacterium is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and produce toxins when cooked rice is left warm for too long.
